entry.title: Headphones
entry.content:
I often walk around town with headphones, listening to music or podcasts. When I take the bus to work, I often read with headphones in tuned to classical music or ambient sounds to drown out the screech of the bus brakes and other passengers. Walking around with music has been a habit since at least college, where I would sneak in a few songs between classes, or walking to/from internships and jobs across D.C. I find taking transit an especially attractive time to pop in audio, where you the passenger can star in a production of life being lived, where the unwitting audience bears tribute to the story inch music serves a fairly epic backdrop. There wasn’t much impetus for the headphones when it started, and listening to something has been an automated habit which I’m sure is not unique to me.

My recent personal milestone was turning thirty. For some reason, the world soon thereafter felt louder and more oppressive. The sound of traffic was amplified. The sensation of the wind through the tree leaves was unignorably loud. I was constantly eavesdropping on conversations I couldn’t bother with. Thinking became tiring, more so than normal. I was becomming overwhelmed by moving through my daily chores because it felt like my sensations were ratcheted up to a level just out of reach of sustainable. So I took the headphones off, and tucked them away until I got home.

My grocery store is a fifteen minute walk away, as is my gym. My office is about a thirty minute bike ride, a bit more by bus. Taking the headphones off and carrying on with my tasks made the tasks feel longer, and more serene. When I feel like I don’t have enough of something, I can’t help on concentrate on my lack of that thing. Having my ears blasted with noise every waking moment made me feel like I was missing silence and stillness and therefore I felt in deep longing. With my naked ears, my life has space to be bored in and space for my thoughts to bounce off the walls of my head again. The fifteen minute walk to the gym or store requries me to look around and take things in as they happen in front of me. There is now no decision to make on what to listen to as the world simply provides. So take the headphones ond stop listening.

entry.title: To be Dumb
entry.content:
I have often thought of myself as the dumb one of the bunch. Assignming myself as the dumb one has carried its way from as early as I can remember, and continues through my present employment. The essay here is not a cry for help, or an invitation to a pity party. The words here are not a flogging, a public display of self deprecation. From conversations I’ve had with loved ones, coworkers, and strangers, I hope nothing I say is controversial in any way and serves only as a musing on what it means to be alive now with just enough knowledge equipped to reckon with the vastness of intelligent space.

It is wholly impossible to measure dumbness. Dumbness is different than anti-intelligence, which is also impossible to measure though we as humans can’t help but try through rituals like IQ tests. Wheras intelligence is possibly some quality of how quickly information leads to knowledge or positive reinforcement, dumbness is a static variable. To be dumb is mortal. To be dumb is inescapable, a force of cosmic goo which grips the ankles and holds on for eternity against the wriggling struggle of those who are dumb and wish not to be.

I want to take the sting out of being dumb, as there is much joy in the dumb brain. Dumbness is not a function of accomplishment. Dumb people do big and great things all the time; through dumbness anything is possible. Take me. Feeling dumb is walking amongst others, being impressed by them. I enjoy being on the bus with what look like many adults, effortlessly shuffling from their homes to their work, conducting calls or their own personal business with skill. I know, I know, I know. Inside the head of all these commuters lives a different, darker reality. My dumb brain tries to play catch up to all these people.

One of, if not the most cliched diagnoses of the current time is “Imposter Syndrome”. I can’t be bothered to look up the origins, but for the unaware Imposter Syndrome is the anxiety associated with one’s perceived professional/social/educational inabilities or lack of skill which a sufferer feels is sure to be brought to light any day now, regardless of any external signals to the contrary. Like most cliches it contains a rich nugget of genuine truth. The truth is people who have “Imposter Syndrome” are not actually dumb, it is instead many of us think we’re dumb.

I refrain from saying I have “Imposter Syndrome”; it feels similar in spirit to the idea of the “Ambivert”, or someone who is neither an extravert nor an introvert: a term borne of finally avoiding saying something definitive. But the truth I can’t hide is my world makes me feel dumb.

Attention is our most valuable asset and currency, and a rich investment in getting attention is to learn to be loud and proud. Once mastered, the can be quite the oyster. Our phones, the ads on every canvasable surface, the buskers on the street are trading their hardened skills for one spec of our precious attention. When our attention is given so freely our eyes get flooded with reminders of how beautiful some people’s voices are, how knowledgable others are on how the world functions, and just how much money there is to go around.

It is an awesome feeling to submit to the dumb brain and casually watch in silence.

My profession is software engineering. I go to my job to write code and talk with people about what they want to do with software I help craft. The advent of LLMs and agentic programming have changed the relationship in style but not necessarily in function. A software engineer if they are worth their weight is going to have to do lots of question asking, clarifying, refinement of goals, and assess quality of varying degrees of tangiblity. Superficially, the “look” of software engineering is clacking away at a keyboard using a monospace font. When I first started coding and programming, it was valuable to know a lot of stuff. It was valuable to know the niches of the library or language you were using or writing with; knowing more meant being able to go faster and deliver something to someone sooner than someone else.

I think the days of defining value that way are over, and have been for a while. Much blog writing has been spilled hashing this same old story again and again. Knowing the technical minutae of a language or library is just only so helpful now that the robots know it all and can regurgitate it faster. And I know the counterpoints about the product an LLM delivers being only superficially good; underneath the shiny surfact is a lot of crap. But our knowledge of numpy, or python’s garbage collection was superficial

Regardless, the firehose of visably functional stuff an LLM pumps out compared to what I can do with my own two hands is at times overpowering. But it’s not what you know, it’s how to think as the adage goes. Then also, it has become time to learn how to architect software from spec; by defining the direction of engineering and system functionalty for the machine, the software engineer keeps his day job. How long will this be the high water mark for the employed and employeable? What are the dumb to do once the tide rises even more?

There was an Atlantic article I read recently asking the nature of what being intelligent means, or meant before AI, and how we apply it on top of these AI machines. The thesis goes roughly like: these machines only mimic real intelligence using some sort of stochastic method, but can’t create intelligence out of thin air the way humans can. It’s an argument that get’s brought up again and again, and the thinking drives me insane. Why is mimicking intelligence not intelligent; is it because mimicking is not creative or destructive? Does it not stand to reason smart people create brilliant things frequently by regurgitating and repetition of honed skills, and then suddenly a novel approach bores itself out. What I find dumb about our use of AI technology is the way we’re holding it. We have a box of all intelligence ready to go, and our wielding of it is to make a chatbot, and do our jobs, the same jobs, the same way we’ve been doing jobs, but faster? We the dumb and brilliant are still so early on this dumb, brilliant technology.

entry.title: The World Cup
entry.content:
One of the movies I have rewatched the most is the official recap documentary of the 2006 World Cup held in Germany. I’m not even sure I’d recommend it, as unless you were a soccer-obsessed child like I was the movie now probably just plays as your typical sizzle reel. But I was a soccer-obsessed child right when the 2006 World Cup was going on, so I was captivated. I really did think Zinedine Zidane was evil to his core, not least because he has such a wickedly evil name, but also because of his famous head butt of some Italian player that I cannot remember, and will not look up. But I grew up, and now think Zidane is super cool, probably BECAUSE his name is so sinister. The 2006 World Cup was around the time I started to engage with players by name, and started to develop a somewhat parasocial relationship with my favorites, especially the US striker Landon Donovan. The guys I watched play were my heroes, and their arenas were inspiring.

One thing about soccer that seems to elude viewers who typically only watch sports like American Football, Basketball, Baseball, etc is that the box score of a soccer game really tells you very little about the reality of the match to a large extent. A 1-1 draw tells you almost nothing about the pacing, the momentum, and the tensions throughout the game. What astounds people is how exciting a 0-0 game can turn out to be, such as the Cape Verde & Spain match most recently. Obviously, it sucks when your country gets knocked out and has to go home, either in the knockout round or in group play. However, watching and experiencing the World Cup is and should be joyful. The pain of getting knocked out is fleeting. Getting knocked out of the World Cup is a singular, miniscule datapoint. Only a vanishingly small minority of countries have won the World Cup ever. It’s not an embarresment to get knocked out.

The joy of the World Cup happens around the edges, like the excitement of the game itself. I love the fans coming from all corners of the earth to depleet a singular country of its beer, food, and attention. I love the idea of a country hosting all other countries, much like the Olympics. For the record, I love the Olympics for all the same reasons as the World Cup, but seeing as I have no personal connection to luge, archery, or the other sports the Olympics serves mostly as a novelty to me. At times my love for the World Cup is ineffible, I simply enjoy the vibe of it all. Other moments are more acute. I love when people represent the prototypical image of their country, like everyone on Croatia’s name ending in -ric. Or Haaland looking legitametly like a viking, and he’s from the viking country! Or the American striker being named “Landon Donovan”. At times the World Cup makes me think our planet is simply a gigantic, casted orchestration and all events are scripted to be perfect for their time. This World Cup presented us with some uniquely American charm, like Lawrence, KS adopting the team from Algeria. When an Algerian news crew interviewed a local Lawrentian about what he thought of Algeria, he gave a cheerful rendition of the top wikipedia bullet points of Algerian history. It almost made me weep. Lawrence, KS should be the capital of the United States.

The World Cup is not without it’s cynics, both within and outside FIFA. I don’t care. Or rather, I don’t dwell on it. FIFA could burn to a smoldering heap of ashes. So long as our world continues to have a hosted series of soccer games where all who are good enough can play, there is something good and great.

entry.title: Reviews
entry.content:
I attended a friend’s wedding a few years ago. Keeping a long story somewhat short, the bride and her brother had hatched a plan for him to propose to his girlfriend right after the ceremony. The plan was for the brother to take the flowers during the bouquet toss while the bridesmaids would step back for the brother to take a knee. It was well orchestrated, the plan went off with just the right hitch in place, and luckily for all of us it was caught on video via an attendee’s cell phone. It was posted online, and at some point soon thereafter went mildly viral. For the record, and to reiterate, the entire plan was done with full consent of the bride, groom, and bridesmaids, and the girlfriend was enthused and totally on board.

The point of the story was the viralness of it, specifically the comments I read. There was no shortage of comments excoriating the brother for how selfish it was to steal the spotlight from the bride. I’m not sure it’s fair to say the response was typical, but it wasn’t abnormal judging. But I was there at the wedding in the flesh. I was with everybody involved in the viral vignette. I knew the backstory, and I knew why they orchestrated the entire ruse in the first place. I reflect on this episode quite a bit when I confront online discourse, especially when it bleeds offline, I find steeped in judgement. The online commenters knew nothing as they weren’t there, and I knew basically everything. But if I didn’t know everything about the story, why wouldn’t my brain be swayed by the judgement of my internet peers? More prescient, what am I currently being swayed by to where I have none of the requisite prior knowledge? Why do we need the opinions of people we don’t know to provide us information they themselves do not know?

iI was talking with my parents a couple of years ago about a promotional feature a now defunct Airline presented frequent fliers. For a reasonable cost, you could purchase a vacation package which included hotel stays, return airline trips, and one or two other nice to haves with the caveat being you, the purchaser of the package, will not know where you are going until you show up to the airport for your flight. I am not sure how much nudging the company would give you in terms of what to pack, what to expect, or if there were any opt-outs with regards to cities which you may be attempting to never go back to.

The concept of jetting off to somewhere, anywhere, is such a romantic and instagram-able bit of consumer behavior it remains the only scene in “Yes Man” starring Jim Carry that I remember. So why aren’t these promotional packages the hot new thing to go viral? My vibe tells me the typical interaction with travel, discourse, and the day to day behaviorisms of of consumption is behind some kind of “review-wall”. The “review-wall” is a shield which protects, contains, and therefore traps against any sort of experimentation with our localisms. The “review-wall” is a muzzle disguised as a megaphone, and through no fault of anyone in particular is likely driving most people just a little mad.

To understand the “review-wall”, go to Google Maps (or Apple Maps, etc). The \Map\ apps provide a forum to review anything, from cafes to natural landmarks. Everything on a map app exists to be judged and rated. These forums are completely public and anyone with an opinion is invited to blast their review out to the world. If a cafe serves you the greatest latte you’ve ever enjoyed, you are often encouraged to post your review on the \Map\ app of your choosing, so other latte enthusiasts can share the experience you’ve just had. Review sites like the \Map\ apps, and Yelp before them, are outstandingly valuable resources for small businesses, which thrive and perish on the backs of upswells of good or bad reviews; that is to say, the “review-wall” is a valuable service with real impact on the way we interact with our communities. One time, after dining in a restaurant and paying for our food, my friends and I shuffled outside. While we are lining up to take a group photo, one of the chefs came outside, took my friends phone, silently went to google maps, and implicitely asking for a high rating showed an un-filled out input form for a review of his restaurant. It was a driven attempt to shake us down for an opinion but it was hard to fault him for his tenacity.

The biggest downside to everyone reviewing everything is the experience I have of being in the same place everywhere. If feels the inevitable outcome of a restaurant is to become Chipotle, shut down, or to already be a beloved neighborhood institution and therefore teeter on until the owners decide to retire. I believe the /Map/ apps exacerbate the sameness, but it would be a mistake to say things are all the same because of the review-wall.

I grew up in Austin, TX, and without any personal bias it is obvious to me the greatest restaurant to ever bless the earth was Magnolia Cafe on Lake Austin Boulevard. The original Magnolia cafe is still on South Congress, though the Lake Austin establishment had home field advantage for me and my fellow West Austinites. It was a 24-hour establishment, had an Escher-like physical layout, and every square inch of touchabel surface was sticky with syrup or some syrup-like residue. The waitstaff did not care if you lived or died, and so tolerated my high school friends, first responders, and meandering vagabonds all the same. The food was good-to-mediocre but plentiful, and I never got the sense anyone left unsatisfied with their meal. Eagle-eyed readers may notice I’m writing in the past tense here, as Lake Austin Mag’s closed in April during the first year of COVID. I wonder if Magnolia could be brought back from the ashes.

Mag’s has since been replaced with a fried chicken chain that is simultaneously delicious and void of a tenth of the heart of it’s ancestral tenant. When I am home, and drive by what used to be Mag’s, the chicken place is packed to the gills with happy customers. So be it, to rail against the existence of trends is an exercise in futility. The \Maps\ reviews of the chicken place are glowing.

To live by the review need not be a requirement. During a summer in college between junior and senior years, I spent time in Alabama on a bird refuge along the Georgia/Alabama state line. The towns along the Chattahoochee corridor were immune the review-wall. In its place was the parking-wall, which was a tecnique bestowed upon me by a rather portly young man I had shadow me at work. He told me:

If you don’t know where to eat, at lunch or dinner time just get in your car and drive around until you find the fullest parking lot you can see, then stop

The technique is not so different than the \Map\ app reviews in a way. To see a full parking lot is an invitation to immerse your own car in the revelry of others.

To be online is to interact with, to various degrees, Reddit. Comments on reddit rise to the top based on the upvote. By default, the comments you see on a post bubble up the most “upvoted” comments, or the highest ratio of “upvote/downvote” (downvote, being the inverse of upvoting). An upvote is a value judgement assigned to a comment. Our forums are based around this concept, where the discussion surfaces the most highly reviewed opinions first. The cream rises to the top. What do we get from this system? A sameness of opinion, a weaving of stories that is only true in the median. The real honest kernals of truth are hidden in the edges where the reality is harder and more opaque. The hard realities are confusing and unpopular. What is popular is easy to digest. And what is easy to digest is what we see copied and pasted ad nausieum.

But again I ask, what is so valuable about the copy and pasted judgements, reviews, and opinions of us all where we are only given such a minisclue sliver of the real meat that what we can posit and post is just hot air? The answer is of course there is nothing valuable to reviews and comments. Listen to your eyes and ears only, believe it if you can see it.

entry.title: Sisters
entry.content:
I guess this one has a build up that I don’t remember. As far as I can recall, I was on a quest to find out where my sisters were and if confronted with their captor, enact my vengance. Hard to imagine myself enacting vengance in real life, but oh well.

I pulled my car into a grove, passing a lot of beat up cars parked alongside a brook, maybe 20 in total. Oak trees were outstretched over the road, shading most of the property. It was quite beautiful, aside from the junk cars, if you could gaze at the main house which resided along a river. The day was muggy and slightly cloudy.

The property owner came out to see who pulled in. He asked quite suspiciously who I was. If I told him, I quickly asked him if he knew where my sisters were. Unclear to me how or why I thought he knew where they would be, I probed and accused more forcefully until he relented. He pointed me to a shack behind the main house and asked me to follow him. Wordlessly he led me to a small footbridge wide enough for only one person at a time. I went first, reaching the other side and sensing his raised fist behind me.

I turned around and caught him migrating his stance from one of threat to a wide outstretched yawn. Clever tactic I suppose. He unlocked the shed. Nothing. I became berzerk, I started throwing fists and we started going at it, dragging each other to the floor. Blow after blow for minutes, until we drain our energies. No upper hand.

“What did you hit me for”, he asked pantingly. “You know where they are” I answereed with all the courage and accusatory force I could find in my psyche between gasps for air.

“I dont even know who you are”

“…”

“Everyone’s a liar”

Hard to know what to make of this one.

entry.title: Rhino
entry.content:
A bit more of a nightmare. It was nighttime and I was hanging with some a handful of others outside the back of the kitchen in Iron City. I had a club or weapon of some kind in my hand and was sort of pacing. I wasn’t nervous, but the mood had a celebatory flavor so it was hard to settle. People were milling about, laughing and goofing off. I looked around and noticed most people, still only a handful at this time, had similar handheld weapons.

Suddenly I got nervous with an impending sense of doom. Something was about to go horribly wrong. The other people around me were beginning to queue up and I shuffled my way in line. After a minute I removed myself and started towards the back, walking around the front of the dining hall until I saw more and more people streaming in from the beach and front lawn, all equiped with makeshift bats, clubs, instruments of damage.

I was almost near the rear of the line before I find the silhouette of the Rhino cast onto the white plaster wall. A cheer rippled through the line and the crowds mood ascended into restless excitment as quickly as mine sank to dread. The rhino was picking people from the line one by one and mauling them into shreds. It didn’t seem to damper the jubliation at all. The clubs were there for the group assault on the rhino but the odds were always stacked against us. Others with grins on their face continued to laugh and play until it was their turn with the beast.

I left the crowd behind and walked along the boardwalk, then hopped off to meander around the rocky shore. A native man I didnt recongnize was smoking on a precipice as the water lapped at his feet. I approached and began making conversation; he wondered why I wasnt with the others. We could still hear them across the water; the night was still and the bay carries sound as if there is no distance.

I said I felt uncomfortable, I guess I wasnt ready to die. He remarked about the ignorance of our clan. I dont know if he was grouping me in with them as well, but I don’t know why he’d exclude me.

I had a club or weapon of some kind in my hand and was sort of pacing. I wasn’t nervous, but the mood had a celebatory flavor so it was hard to settle. People were milling about, laughing and goofing off. I looked around and noticed most people, still only a handful at this time, had similar handheld weapons.
